Sanvad AI: What Counts as Resolved

A teaching case. Sanvad AI and Khaleej Freightways are fictional companies; the regulators, platforms and Indian market around them are real.

1. Sunday night, Besant Nagar

At half past eleven on the night of Sunday, 15 March 2026, Devika Sundaresan sat at the dining table of her flat off Elliot's Beach Road in Chennai with four printouts spread in front of her and a fifth still in the printer. The board pre-read was due at nine the next morning. The board met on Thursday. The renewal term sheet for Khaleej Freightways, Sanvad AI's largest customer, had to go out by 31 March.

Devika had been Chief Product Officer of Sanvad AI for two years and four months. In that time the company's single most quoted number — the auto-resolution rate, the share of customer-support conversations its AI closed without a human agent — had gone from 39 percent to 63 percent, and that curve had appeared on the first page of the Series C deck, in two trade-press profiles, in the compensation plan of the engineering organisation in Pune, and in Schedule 3 of the Khaleej Freightways contract, where it carried a service-credit clause.

The four printouts, read together, made it unclear what the number meant. One of them, if taken at face value, implied that the true figure was somewhere in the low forties and had been for eighteen months. Another implied it was higher than 63 percent. Devika did not think either was obviously wrong, and she did not have a way to decide between them before nine o'clock.

2. Company history, and the decision that constrains it

Sanvad AI was founded in Chennai in 2019 by Raghav Iyengar and two colleagues from a large Indian IT services firm, on the observation that Indian software companies had learned to sell support tooling to the world — Freshworks and Zoho had proved the market — but that nobody was selling support outcomes. Sanvad's product sat on top of an existing helpdesk, read the customer's knowledge base and past tickets, and answered incoming conversations itself. It charged per conversation resolved, not per agent seat.

By March 2026 the company had ₹86 crore of annual recurring revenue, 41 enterprise accounts and about 610 mid-market ones, 340 employees, and a Series C of ₹410 crore raised in August 2024 at a valuation of ₹2,900 crore. Engineering was split between Bengaluru, where the retrieval and platform teams sat, and Pune, where the model team had grown around two early hires. Design was led from Berlin, data science from Toronto, customer success from Singapore, and enterprise sales from Edison, New Jersey.

One decision from 2024 constrains everything Devika can do now. Until 30 June 2024, "auto-resolved" meant exactly one thing: a conversation that closed without any human agent sending a message. On 1 July 2024, following a product council note argued by the Pune model team and approved by Devika's predecessor in her last week, the definition was broadened to include a second case — a conversation in which a human agent accepted Sanvad's suggested reply and sent it without editing it. The reasoning in the note was defensible: an agent who accepts a suggestion verbatim has been relieved of the work, and the value created is the same. The note estimated the impact at "three to four percentage points, immaterial." Nobody revisited the contract schedules, which had been drafted against the older definition in June 2022 and simply referenced "conversations auto-resolved as computed by the Supplier's platform."

3. The industry

Sanvad sold into a market that had become crowded and loud within two years. Indian buyers — a private bank, two brokers, a quick-commerce company, a large paints manufacturer's dealer-support desk — bought on cost per contact, and every one of them benchmarked Sanvad against the incumbent helpdesk vendors they already used. Overseas buyers, who supplied 58 percent of revenue, bought on headcount avoidance and were more willing to sign outcome-based pricing.

Three external forces bore directly on measurement. First, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the consent architecture Sanvad's Indian clients had built around it, meant that Sanvad could not freely obtain the downstream record of what happened to an end customer after a conversation closed; access had to be provided by the client, for a stated purpose, and only nine of the 41 enterprise accounts had agreed to share it. Second, the private bank client, being an RBI-regulated entity, imposed outsourcing terms that limited conversation-log retention to ninety days, which meant that any historical restatement was arithmetically impossible for that account. Third, inference costs had become a first-order line item: the 2025 shift to longer retrieval contexts and automatic retries had raised Sanvad's cost per resolved conversation by nearly a fifth, and export invoicing under GST rules for services meant the margin was visible to the finance team monthly and to the board quarterly.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence, as Devika reconstructed it over the previous fortnight, ran as follows.

In February 2024 the board had asked for a single product metric and had been given the auto-resolution rate. It was a reasonable choice at the time: it was a ratio, so it was not merely a report on how much traffic customers happened to send; it was observable within a day; and it mapped onto the pitch the sales team made. Meenal Deshpande's model organisation in Pune had its quarterly bonus pool tied to it from April 2024.

On 1 July 2024 the definition broadened. What was believed then was that accepted-suggestion conversations were a small and roughly constant slice. What has since turned out to be wrong is the "roughly constant" part. Agent-assist adoption grew far faster than autonomous resolution, partly because Sanvad's own product decisions made accepting a suggestion the path of least resistance — one keystroke, default-focused — and partly because enterprise clients found accepted suggestions easier to govern than fully autonomous replies. By the December 2025 quarter, accepted-suggestion conversations accounted for 18.7 of the 63.0 percentage points.

In November 2025 Anand Venkatraman's team in Toronto built a detector that flagged whether an end customer came back within seventy-two hours with a conversation about the same topic. Run on the nine accounts that shared downstream data, it found a reopen rate on auto-resolved conversations of 31.0 percent, against 8.4 percent for conversations a human had closed. Anand circulated it internally on 24 November with a one-line caveat about threshold sensitivity that most readers skipped.

On 31 January 2026 Grace Lim's customer-success team in Singapore delivered a manual audit of 400 auto-resolved conversations, graded by two analysts against a rubric Grace had written. Seventy-one percent were graded "genuinely resolved". The audit was commissioned to answer the reopen finding and was delivered in five working days.

On 18 February 2026, Rizwan Shaikh, Director of Customer Operations at Khaleej Freightways in Dubai, wrote to Sanvad's account team asking for "the workbook behind the Schedule 3 computation, with the definition of the numerator as applied each quarter since FY24." He did not say why he was asking. Bhaskar Nadkarni, the sales head in New Jersey, forwarded the mail to Devika with the words "handle with care" and no other comment.

On 4 March 2026, Tobias Krämer in Berlin circulated a three-page proposal to redefine resolution from the end customer's point of view — a conversation counts as resolved if the customer neither returns nor rates the interaction poorly within seven days. Devika learned on 11 March that Tobias had already shown a version of the proposal to a design contact at a prospective European client.

5. The people

Raghav Iyengar, co-founder and CEO, Chennai. Position: the number is not wrong, it is differently defined, and a footnote is sufficient. Incentive: a secondary sale in a Series D round he expects to open in June, priced off the growth story the rate underwrites. Not saying: he has already committed the 63 percent figure verbally to two prospective lead investors.

Devika Sundaresan, Chief Product Officer, Chennai. Position: undecided, which is the problem. Incentive: she inherited the definition change and did not make it, but she has presented the series four times since. Not saying: she has not yet told Raghav what the restated figure would be.

Meenal Deshpande, VP Engineering, Pune. Position: the model is genuinely much better than it was in 2024, the reopen analysis is an artefact of a badly chosen similarity threshold, and a restatement would demoralise forty engineers who did real work. Incentive: her organisation's bonus pool is tied to the rate. Not saying: she knows that the default-focused accept button, shipped in September 2024 by her platform team, materially raised the accepted-suggestion share.

Anand Venkatraman, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the company should validate the resolution signal against a downstream outcome and stop arguing from intuition. Incentive: a validated measurement framework is his mandate and his promotion case. Not saying: the automated grader his team built to score resolution quality was trained on the same conversation logs as the production model and shares its failure modes, so its agreement with the model is partly circular.

Grace Lim, Customer Success lead, Singapore. Position: the 71 percent audit figure is the most honest number in the building because a human read every conversation. Incentive: her team's renewal targets depend on the enterprise accounts not reopening the pricing conversation. Not saying: to deliver by 31 January she let her analysts draw the sample from the six accounts whose logs were easiest to access, all of them English-language desks.

Bhaskar Nadkarni, Head of Enterprise Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Position: no metric change before the 31 March quarter close, under any circumstances. Incentive: 44 percent of his variable compensation lands on FY26 bookings. Not saying: a competitor has begun quoting a stricter, customer-verified definition to his largest live prospect, and he has been unable to answer it.

Tobias Krämer, Design Lead, Berlin. Position: the whole argument is downstream of a bad construct; resolution is a thing that happens to a customer, not a state of a ticket. Incentive: the redefinition is his idea and would make design central to measurement. Not saying: his proposal, applied to FY26 Q3, produces a number he has not yet computed.

Rizwan Shaikh, Director of Customer Operations, Khaleej Freightways, Dubai. Position: has asked only for the workbook. Incentive: he is under instruction to reduce outsourced support cost by 15 percent in the coming financial year. Not saying: his procurement team has calculated a credit exposure under Schedule 3 and is holding it in reserve.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Sanvad AI: conversations and reported auto-resolution rate, FY25 Q1 to FY26 Q3
QuarterIngested (crore)Auto-resolved (crore)Reported rateRate on 2021 definition
FY25 Q12.420.9539.3%39.3%
FY25 Q22.711.2245.0%40.6%
FY25 Q33.101.4948.1%41.2%
FY25 Q43.621.8851.9%41.9%
FY26 Q14.102.2554.9%42.6%
FY26 Q24.662.7559.0%43.5%
FY26 Q35.213.2863.0%44.3%

The final column is a reconstruction produced by the Bengaluru platform team on 9 March 2026 by re-running the older rule over retained logs. It excludes the RBI-regulated bank account, whose logs are deleted at ninety days, and therefore covers 94 percent of volume; the team has flagged that the exclusion may bias the column by up to 1.5 pp in either direction. "Ingested" counts every inbound conversation object created, including automated notifications and duplicate threads; a Bengaluru ticket filed in January 2026 estimates that such traffic grew from 4 percent to 11 percent of volume over the period and has not been excluded from any column. Source: Sanvad AI platform warehouse.

Exhibit 1 is the exhibit the board has seen, except for the last column, which it has not. Read across the top row and the bottom row, the two columns tell incompatible stories: one shows a product that has improved by 24 percentage points in seven quarters, the other a product that has improved by five. The footnote introduces a third possibility, in the opposite direction: if the denominator has been inflated by automated traffic that no reasonable person would expect an AI to resolve, then both columns understate the product.

Exhibit 2. Reopen analysis, nine accounts sharing downstream data, October–December 2025
Closure typeConversations (lakh)Reopened < 72 hReopen rate
Auto-resolved (current definition)41.612.931.0%
— of which autonomous28.910.134.9%
— of which accepted suggestion12.72.822.0%
Human-resolved24.42.08.4%

"Same topic" is determined by cosine similarity of conversation embeddings above 0.82, a threshold selected by the Toronto data team in November 2025 by inspecting fifty examples. Sensitivity: at a threshold of 0.90 the auto-resolved reopen rate is 19.4 percent; at 0.75 it is 44.1 percent. The nine participating accounts are all non-Indian, because the DPDP Act consent flow for downstream sharing was still being drafted with Indian clients as of March 2026; these nine are also, by revenue, Sanvad's nine largest. Source: Toronto data science, 24 November 2025.

Exhibit 2 is the printout that had kept Devika at the table. If a third of auto-resolved conversations come back, the rate is not measuring resolution. But the sensitivity footnote spans 19.4 to 44.1 percent, which is the difference between an irritant and a crisis, and the nine accounts are the largest and least representative in the book.

Exhibit 3. Manual audit of 400 auto-resolved conversations, delivered 31 January 2026

Genuinely resolved28471.0%
Partially resolved6215.5%
Not resolved4110.3%
Cannot tell from the transcript133.3%

Sample drawn from six accounts; 92 percent of sampled conversations were in English, against 54 percent of Sanvad's total conversation volume. Two graders; Cohen's kappa on a 60-conversation overlap was 0.41. Graders were aware which conversations were autonomous and which were accepted suggestions. Source: Customer Success, Singapore.

Exhibit 3 was commissioned to rebut Exhibit 2 and is cited in the building as if it had. Whether it does depends on whether one believes that two graders who agreed only moderately with each other, working on a convenience sample of English conversations from the easiest six accounts, measured the same thing that the embedding detector measured on the nine largest.

Exhibit 4. Unit economics of the resolution line, ₹ per auto-resolved conversation

Revenue per resolution (₹)6.905.10−26.1%

Revenue per resolution falls because enterprise contracts carry committed-volume tiers. Cost excludes the retry budget for conversations that escalate to a human, which the Pune team books to platform overhead rather than to the resolution line; finance estimates that reallocation would add ₹0.31 per resolution. Source: Sanvad AI finance, 28 February 2026.

Exhibit 4 is the exhibit nobody in the metric argument has read carefully. It says that the magnitude is doing exactly what the business needs — resolutions more than doubled and line revenue rose 62 percent — while the economics of each unit deteriorated badly. It also says that if the restated numerator is right, Sanvad has been billing for a category of work whose cost it can measure and whose value it cannot.

Exhibit 5. Khaleej Freightways: contract and credit exposure

Schedule 3 says the numerator is "conversations auto-resolved as computed by the Supplier's platform." Sanvad's external counsel in Mumbai advised on 10 March that the clause is capable of both readings and that retrospective application would turn on whether the 2024 change was a computation change or a definition change. The cap has never been tested. Source: contract abstract prepared by Sanvad legal.

Exhibit 6. Competitive benchmark, from a channel partner's deck, February 2026

Methodology not disclosed for any vendor. The figures for Vendors A and B are taken from their public marketing pages, both dated 2024. The partner that produced the deck also resells Vendor B. Sanvad's figure was supplied by Sanvad's own marketing team. Source: partner deck circulated by Bhaskar Nadkarni, 19 February 2026.

Exhibit 6 appears in every Sanvad sales deck. It is also the exhibit that would be most damaged by a restatement, since 44.3 percent would place Sanvad exactly level with a competitor's two-year-old marketing claim.

7. Voices

"We did not change the truth, we changed the accounting. An agent who presses accept has been helped. That is the product working. If we restate now we are telling the market we cannot count, which is a worse story than any number."

Raghav Iyengar, CEO, product council, Chennai, 6 March 2026

"Threshold 0.82 was chosen by looking at fifty tickets on a Tuesday. Please do not build a restatement on it. Give me six weeks and a labelled set and I will give you a number you can defend. What I cannot give you is a number by Monday."

Anand Venkatraman, Head of Data Science, Toronto, internal message, 9 March 2026, 06:14 IST

"Forty people in Pune shipped grounded retrieval, the escalation classifier and the Hindi and Tamil models in eighteen months. The rate went up because the product got better. I am not going to walk into a team meeting and say the last two years were a measurement artefact, because that is not what happened."

Meenal Deshpande, VP Engineering, Pune, engineering all-hands, 10 March 2026

"My analysts read four hundred conversations. Seventy-one percent were fine. I understand the embeddings are interesting but a human being read the actual transcript. Also, for what it is worth, three of my nine enterprise accounts have asked what 'resolved' means in the last month, unprompted."

Grace Lim, Customer Success, Singapore, email to Devika, 11 March 2026

"We are arguing about the numerator of a fraction whose denominator includes eleven percent machine-generated noise, and neither number has ever been shown to a customer. Ask Rizwan what he thinks resolved means. I did, informally, in January. His answer was 'my agent never touches it and the driver stops calling.'"

Tobias Krämer, Design Lead, Berlin, comment on the redefinition proposal, 4 March 2026

"Whatever you decide, decide it on 1 April. Two weeks. That is all I am asking."

Bhaskar Nadkarni, Head of Enterprise Sales, Edison, voice note, 13 March 2026

8. The options as Devika sees them

Hold. Report 63.0 percent to the board with a footnote describing the July 2024 change, renew Khaleej Freightways on the existing Schedule 3, and commission Anand's six-week validation study. The case for it is that no external party has yet asked a question Sanvad cannot answer, and that a restatement announced without a defensible replacement number is the worst of both worlds. The case against it is that Rizwan's request for the workbook is precisely such a question, and that it has been sitting unanswered for four weeks.

Restate. Publish both columns of Exhibit 1, take the credit exposure, and reset the sales narrative around 44.3 percent with an honest trajectory. The case for it is that the restatement will happen eventually and that doing it before a Series D is cheaper than during one. The case against it is that 44.3 percent is not obviously more true than 63.0 percent — it is merely older, it excludes the bank account, and it sits on the same inflated denominator.

Split. Report two series, autonomous resolution and assisted resolution, with separate rates and separate prices, and move Khaleej to the autonomous series at renewal. The case for it is that it dissolves the definitional dispute by refusing to add unlike things. The case against it is that the assisted series is the faster-growing one, so splitting it out invites the question of what it is worth, which nobody at Sanvad can currently answer.

Devika had written the three options on a single sheet, and had then written underneath, in the margin: all three of these are arguments about a rate. The magnitude — 3.28 crore resolutions, ₹16.7 crore of line revenue, more than doubled in a year — is not in dispute in any of them, and it is the number the company is actually paid for. Nor does any of the three address what Tobias had put his finger on: that no version of the numerator has ever been anchored to anything that happens to an end customer, and that the denominator has been quietly drifting for two years. She was not sure whether that made the three options wrong or merely incomplete, and she was not sure the distinction mattered by nine o'clock.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board pre-read is due at 09:00 IST on Monday, 16 March 2026, and the board meets on Thursday, 19 March, with two investor directors attending from London and Singapore. The Khaleej Freightways term sheet must go out by 31 March; the account is 17.0 percent of ARR and its credit exposure is between ₹0.91 crore and ₹3.65 crore depending on a contract reading that counsel will not settle. Cash is not the binding constraint — the company held ₹268 crore at the end of February — but the FY27 plan assumes 38 percent net revenue retention expansion in the top ten accounts, eight of which are on outcome pricing tied to some version of this definition.

Anand's validation study needs six weeks and a labelled set that, for Indian accounts, cannot lawfully be built until the DPDP consent flow ships, which engineering has scheduled for May. The bank account's logs are gone at ninety days, so any restatement is permanently partial. Meenal's bonus pool for the year closes on 31 March. And Bhaskar has four enterprise deals worth ₹19 crore of ARR in commit for the quarter, all of them with Exhibit 6 in the deck.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Write down, in one sentence and without using the word "resolved", what Sanvad AI's customers are actually buying. Then list every number in Exhibits 1 to 6 and say how far each sits from that thing.

2. Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 imply different answers to the same question. For each, identify what is being counted, what it is being divided by, and the one assumption that would have to hold for it to mean what its author intends.

3. The footnote to Exhibit 1 says automated traffic grew from 4 to 11 percent of ingested conversations. Work out roughly what excluding it would do to the reported rate, and decide whether excluding it would make the metric better or merely more flattering. How would you tell the difference?

4. Exhibit 4 shows the magnitude doubling while the margin per unit collapses. If Sanvad had been managing to a magnitude rather than a rate for the past two years, which of its present problems would it have avoided, and which new ones would it have?

5. The July 2024 change was approved as a "computation change" in a product council note. What governance would have caught it, who should have owned the definition, and what does it cost to put that governance in now, mid-quarter, with bonuses closing on 31 March?

6. What should Devika do on Monday morning — what goes in the pre-read, what does she say to Rizwan Shaikh, and what does she tell the board on Thursday about a number she has presented four times? If the board asks her directly whether the company has been reporting a metric that overstates its product, what is her answer?

Besant Nagar, 01:15

By a quarter past one Devika had three versions of the first pre-read page. The first began with the 63.0 percent figure and a footnote. The second began with both columns of Exhibit 1 side by side and no commentary. The third began with a sentence she had typed and not yet deleted: We have been reporting a rate whose numerator we changed and whose denominator we did not examine, and I do not yet know what the right number is.

She thought about Rizwan's phrase — my agent never touches it and the driver stops calling — and about the fact that Sanvad had built a ₹86-crore business without ever once measuring whether the driver stopped calling. She thought about Meenal's forty engineers, who had in fact built something good, and about the two prospective lead investors who had heard 63 percent from Raghav's own mouth. Outside, the last of the traffic on Elliot's Beach Road had gone quiet. The printer had finished. Devika read the third version again, then moved the cursor to the beginning of the sentence and left it there.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Direct vs Proxy, Magnitude vs Ratio

1. A board meeting in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March 2026, Meher Vashisht, VP of Product at the fitness app Zindagi Fit, stood in front of the company's board with a slide she had rewritten four times the night before. Zindagi Fit had closed its Series B seven months earlier, and the board — including its lead investor Rajan Sabharwal, who had flown in from Mumbai for the meeting — wanted one number: was the ₹4 crore spent on February's performance-marketing push working. Meher's dashboard said yes: app opens were up 52% month over month, and weekly active users, the metric the growth team had promised the board it would move, was up 32%. Rajan smiled. Then Zindagi Fit's data lead, Kabir Anand, who worked out of Pune and had dialled in, asked a question that emptied the room of confidence: of the users who opened the app in February, what fraction actually finished a workout, and had that fraction gone up or down? Meher did not know. She knew opens. She knew active users. She did not, in that room, know whether the marketing push had brought people who used Zindagi Fit for fitness or people who used it for a free trial and a notification badge. The distinction was not academic — the board was about to decide whether to double the marketing budget for Q2, and the answer depended on which of several numbers on Meher's slide actually measured what Zindagi Fit was selling: fitness, not attention.

Figure 1 — the same month, told three ways.

2. The idea

A direct metric measures the outcome you actually care about. A proxy metric measures something else, chosen because the outcome itself is hard, slow, or expensive to observe, and offered up as a stand-in on the strength of a believed correlation with the outcome. Separately, a magnitude is a raw count or sum — opens, rupees, minutes, users — while a ratio normalises one quantity by another — opens per install, minutes per active user, conversions per hundred visits. The two distinctions are independent of each other: you can have a direct magnitude (total workouts completed), a direct ratio (workouts completed per active user), a proxy magnitude (total app opens), or a proxy ratio (opens per install). Confusing the two axes — treating "proxy" and "magnitude" as the same failure — is itself one of the most common errors in this space, and section 5 returns to it.

The vocabulary was not born in a product team. Web analysts in the early 2000s, working with server logs that could count almost anything, needed language for the fact that a count could be large and meaningless at once; Avinash Kaushik's writing on "vanity metrics" versus "actionable metrics" popularised the idea that a number should be judged by whether it changes a decision, not by how impressive it looks on a dashboard. Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz, in Lean Analytics (2013), pushed this further by insisting that ratios — rates and per-user figures — are usually the ones that inform action, because they survive changes in scale that make raw counts drift for reasons unrelated to the decision at hand. The GAME framework that this topic sits under treats this as its metric step: once you have named the goal and the action that signals it, you must still decide how that action gets counted and normalised, and that is exactly the direct-versus-proxy, magnitude-versus-ratio choice. The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without flinching is this: we count the action closest to the outcome we're paid for, and we report it as a rate before we report it as a number.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and the order matters because skipping a step is exactly how teams end up defending a metric they cannot justify under questioning. First, name the true outcome in business terms — for Zindagi Fit, a member who exercises regularly and renews their subscription. Second, ask whether that outcome is directly observable at the cadence a decision needs. "Renewed" is directly observable, but only once a year per user, far too slow to steer February's marketing spend. So a nearer, faster signal is needed — a proxy — and the discipline is to state, out loud, the causal story connecting the proxy to the outcome: a member who completes workouts regularly is more likely to renew, based on Zindagi Fit's own cohort data from 2024–25. Third, decide the numerator: not "the app opened" but "a workout was marked complete," because completion, not launch, is what the causal story actually claims. Fourth, decide the denominator: completed workouts alone will simply grow whenever the user base grows, so a ratio — completed workouts divided by weekly active users — is needed to see whether engagement per person is improving or merely riding a bigger crowd. Fifth, assign a cadence and an owner: Zindagi Fit reviews this ratio weekly, and Kabir's analytics pod owns the number, meaning they can be asked to defend it. Sixth — the step practitioners most often skip — periodically re-test whether the proxy still tracks the outcome, because a signal chosen in 2024 can quietly stop meaning what it once meant as the product, the user base, or a competitor's move changes underneath it.

4. A worked example

Zindagi Fit's February 2026 numbers: 9,20,000 app opens, 46,000 weekly active users (WAU), and 1,84,000 completed workouts. The ratio the team now insists on is completed workouts divided by WAU: 1,84,000 ÷ 46,000 = 4.00 workouts per active user for the month. In March, after the ₹4 crore marketing push, app opens rose to 14,00,000 (+52%) and WAU rose to 61,000 (+32%) — the two numbers Meher first presented, both moving the right way. But completed workouts rose only to 2,00,000, an increase of 8.7%. The ratio for March is 2,00,000 ÷ 61,000 = 3.28 workouts per active user — a drop of 18% from February's 4.00.

Figure 2 — every headline number improved; the one direct ratio did not.

Change one input and the story sharpens further. Suppose the marketing team had instead spent the same ₹4 crore on a channel that brought fewer but higher-intent sign-ups, so that March WAU rose only to 50,000 (+8.7%, matching workout growth) while completed workouts still reached 2,00,000. The ratio would then be 2,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 4.00 — unchanged from February. Same marketing spend, same completed-workout magnitude, wildly different verdict on whether the campaign worked, because the second scenario grew the denominator no faster than the numerator. This is the entire argument in one number: a magnitude going up tells you activity is growing somewhere; a ratio going up or down tells you whether it is growing where you wanted it to.

5. The nuances

Direct and proxy are a spectrum, not a label. "Completed workout" is more direct than "app open" but still a proxy for the outcome Zindagi Fit is ultimately paid for, which is a member's sustained fitness and renewal. Every metric a team reports is a proxy for something further downstream; the question is never "is this a proxy" but "how many inferential steps separate this number from the decision it's meant to inform."

A rising ratio can hide a collapsing denominator. If WAU had fallen from 46,000 to 30,000 while completed workouts fell only to 1,50,000, the ratio would rise to 5.00 — an apparent improvement produced entirely by losing casual users, not by engaging anyone more deeply. A ratio is only as trustworthy as the story behind both the numerator and the denominator moving.

The choice of denominator changes the verdict. Workouts per WAU, per MAU, and per install are three different ratios that can move in three different directions in the same month, because each denominator answers a different question — engagement of the active core, engagement of the wider base, or efficiency of acquisition. Naming the denominator is not a formality; it is half the definition of the metric.

Proxies decay. A signal that tracked the true outcome faithfully in 2024 can stop doing so once users learn what is being measured, once a feature changes what "opening the app" even means, or once a competitor changes user behaviour industry-wide. This is the practical form of Goodhart's law: a measure that becomes a target for a bonus or a headline stops being a reliable measure. Re-testing the proxy against the real outcome, on some fixed cadence, is not optional maintenance — it is the only thing standing between the team and a comfortable, wrong number.

Magnitude still matters, even when a ratio is the decision metric. Zindagi Fit's finance team needs total completed workouts, not the ratio, to plan server capacity and instructor payouts; a ratio of 3.28 tells the product team about engagement quality but tells nobody how many workouts the infrastructure must serve. The two axes answer different questions and a mature team reports both, deliberately, rather than picking one as if the other did not exist.

Correlation with the proxy is not causation of the outcome. That heavy app-openers renew more often does not prove that opening the app more will make anyone renew; the causal arrow may run the other way; a member who has already decided to stay may simply open the app more out of habit. Treating a proxy as a lever to be pulled, rather than a signal to be read, is where many well-intentioned metric programmes go wrong.

Small denominators make ratios noisy. A new city launch with 40 weekly active users can swing "workouts per WAU" from 3.0 to 5.0 on the strength of a handful of enthusiastic early adopters; that swing is sampling noise, not a signal to act on, and a ratio needs a minimum base before anyone should trust its movement.

A ratio cannot tell you why it moved. Knowing that workouts per WAU fell from 4.00 to 3.28 does not say whether new users are less committed, whether an app update broke a feature, or whether a competitor launched a cheaper plan. The ratio flags where to look; a segmented breakdown by cohort, channel, or app version is what answers why.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

In a consumer product like Zindagi Fit, the natural denominator is a user — per-user ratios such as workouts per WAU are the default because the population of individual consumers is large and comparable. In a B2B product, the natural denominator is often an account or a seat, and the direct outcome sits further away in time: a project-management tool cares less about "logins per user" than about "tasks completed per active team," because the renewal decision is made by an account, not an individual. In a marketplace, both sides need their own ratio — a food-delivery platform tracks orders completed per active customer and, separately, orders fulfilled per active restaurant partner, and a healthy marketplace requires both to hold up, not just one. Scale changes the calculus too: an early-stage company, with a few hundred users, often has no honest choice but to lean on proxies and even raw magnitudes, because the true outcome — renewal, referral, lifetime value — has not yet had time to occur often enough to measure directly; a large company with years of history can and should tie its proxies back to validated outcome data on a fixed schedule, precisely the discipline Kabir's team was pushing Zindagi Fit toward in year two of its life.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is reporting a magnitude and calling it engagement — the symptom is a dashboard full of numbers that only ever go up, and the underlying error is that a growing user base will lift almost any raw count regardless of what individual users are doing; the cheapest diagnostic is to divide every headline magnitude by active users before presenting it. The second is adopting a proxy without ever stating the causal claim behind it — the symptom is a team that cannot answer "why do we believe this predicts the outcome," and the diagnostic is simply asking that question in the room before the metric goes on a dashboard. The third is letting a ratio's denominator drift unnoticed, for instance quietly switching from per-WAU to per-MAU between quarters to flatter a trend — the symptom is a metric that looks stable while underlying behaviour is not, and the diagnostic is a metric dictionary that pins the exact denominator and requires sign-off to change it. The fourth is trusting a ratio computed on a small or newly launched segment — the symptom is a number that jumps wildly week to week — and the diagnostic is a minimum sample-size threshold below which the ratio is reported with a confidence band or not reported as a headline at all.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, Zindagi Fit's monthly board deck opens with a single small table, not a wall of charts: total completed workouts as the magnitude for capacity planning, completed workouts per WAU as the ratio for engagement quality, and a one-line note on any change to WAU's definition since the previous board meeting. Kabir's team re-validates the workouts-to-renewal link every quarter against the prior year's actual renewal data, and flags publicly the quarter it weakened after a pricing change altered who signed up in the first place. When Rajan Sabharwal asks a question in a board meeting now, Meher can answer it from the table itself, because the table was built to answer exactly that kind of question rather than to look impressive.

9. What Meher decided

Meher recommended, and the board accepted, that Zindagi Fit retire app opens as a headline metric, keep weekly active users as a magnitude context figure only, and adopt completed workouts per WAU as the primary metric for judging both product changes and marketing spend, reported alongside total completed workouts for operational planning. The reasoning she gave was the one this page has walked through: a number that can rise while the thing the company sells is falling is not a metric a serious team should let steer money. What she asked Kabir's team to build next was cohort-level retention curves segmented by acquisition channel, so that a falling ratio could be traced to a cause rather than merely observed. Two questions worth sitting with: when you last defended a metric in a meeting, could you have named its denominator without checking a dashboard — and is there a proxy on your own team's scorecard whose causal link to the real outcome nobody has re-tested this year?

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Direct vs Proxy, Magnitude vs Ratio

How each action gets counted and normalised — and why two competent practitioners can look at the same data and reach opposite verdicts.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 14 January 2026, in a converted bungalow off Bengaluru's Kanakapura Road, Anuradha Rau, VP of Product at Gulmohar Learning, was arguing with her own chief financial officer about a number neither of them disputed. Gulmohar sold an exam-preparation subscription to 3,10,000 paying students, most in Tier-2 towns preparing for NEET and the JEE cycle, at ₹2,400 a year. Annual renewal — the number the business lived on — stood at 41%. But renewal is observed once per student per year, and Anuradha's roadmap committee met fortnightly: eleven months of silence between decision and outcome. So the team steered on study minutes: 48 per paying subscriber per week, up from 44 a year earlier. The CFO wanted total minutes on the board slide, because totals had grown 31% while the ratio grew 9%. Anuradha wanted mock tests completed per subscriber per week — 0.62, down from 0.71 — because Gulmohar's back-test showed mock-test frequency separated renewers from churners far more sharply than minutes did. The disagreement was not about arithmetic. It was about which number was permitted to kill a feature.

Nine days later and 840 kilometres north, Suhel Qureshi, head of product at Hiranya Field Cloud in Gurugram, faced the mirror image. Hiranya sold field-service software to 41 enterprise accounts — appliance-service networks, lift-maintenance firms, a diagnostics chain — covering 11,800 licensed technician seats, 7,100 active in a typical week. Renewal here was a negotiation with a named procurement head, turning on whether the customer believed Hiranya had raised technician throughput. Suhel's dashboard said work orders closed had risen from 3,62,000 to 3,86,000 in a quarter. His data scientist in Kochi, Meenal Thampi, had a different slide: closes per active technician per day had fallen from 4.00 to 3.63. Both were correct. The contract at stake was ₹6.2 crore. Suhel had to choose which number to put in front of the customer, knowing their analytics team would eventually compute the other one.

Figure 1 — Anuradha's problem is that the outcome is too slow to steer by; Suhel's is that two honest countings of the same quarter point in opposite directions.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Two distinctions are in play, and they are orthogonal. A direct metric measures the outcome the business is actually paid for; a proxy metric measures something nearer in time or cheaper to observe, offered as a stand-in on the strength of an asserted causal or predictive link. Separately, a magnitude is a raw count or sum, while a ratio normalises one quantity by another. Minutes studied is a proxy magnitude; minutes per subscriber is a proxy ratio; renewal count is a direct magnitude; renewal rate is a direct ratio. Most bad metric arguments are two arguments wearing one coat: one side objects to proxy-ness, the other to normalisation, and neither notices.

The proxy problem has an older and more rigorous literature than product management usually admits. Clinical statistics reached it first: a drug trial cannot wait fifteen years for mortality data, so it uses a surrogate endpoint — cholesterol, tumour shrinkage — and Ross Prentice's 1989 criterion set the bar for when that is legitimate. A surrogate is valid, on Prentice's account, only if the treatment's effect on the true outcome is entirely captured by its effect on the surrogate: conditional on the surrogate, the treatment must have no residual effect. The criterion is demanding and famously often violated — the CAST trial of the late 1980s found drugs that improved the surrogate while increasing mortality. Economics arrived independently: Athey, Chetty, Imbens and Kang's surrogate index (2019) showed that a weighted combination of short-run signals estimates a long-run outcome more reliably than any single one. Product management's own tradition is thinner: Avinash Kaushik's vanity-versus-actionable distinction, Croll and Yoskovitz's insistence in Lean Analytics (2013) that rates beat counts, and Ronny Kohavi's account of why Bing's experimentation programme settled on sessions-per-user rather than revenue-per-search — degrading relevance reliably raises queries per session, and revenue with them, in exactly the way that destroys the business. Hovering over all of it is Goodhart's 1975 observation and Campbell's parallel law: a measure adopted as a target ceases to be a good measure.

Four positions can be stated cleanly, and each has practitioners who would sign it in writing. The surrogate-engineering school holds that a validated composite proxy is superior to a slow direct outcome, because it is sensitive enough to adjudicate individual product changes; it will sign "a proxy whose predictive validity we re-estimate quarterly is a better decision instrument than a renewal number we see once a year," and refuse to sign "the proxy is the goal." The outcome-fundamentalist school, strongest among founders and finance leaders, will sign "if it is not in the P&L it is a hypothesis," and refuse to sign "an engagement ratio may override a revenue decline." The ratio-first school holds that unnormalised counts drift with scale; it will sign "report no magnitude without its denominator," and refuse to sign "magnitudes are useless" — capacity, payroll and unit economics run on magnitudes. The mix-sceptic school, which grows stronger the larger the company, holds that a blended ratio can move opposite to every one of its parts; it will sign "no ratio without a segment decomposition beside it," and refuse to sign "therefore report totals." Anuradha belongs to the first school by temperament; her CFO to the second; Meenal Thampi, in Kochi, to the fourth.

3. Mechanics in depth

The expert procedure has six steps, of which three are usually left implicit and are precisely where teams go wrong.

Step one: write the outcome as an equation, not a word. Gulmohar's outcome is not "engagement" but annual revenue retention: subscribers × renewal rate × average realised price. Written this way, it shows which terms a product change can touch. Step two: measure the lag. A proxy is licensed only where the outcome's observation lag exceeds the decision cadence. Gulmohar: eleven months against a fortnight — licensed. Hiranya: renewal is negotiated, with leading indicators visible inside the account, so the lag is shorter and the licence weaker. Step three — the step usually skipped — is to quantify the proxy's predictive validity rather than assert it. Meenal's method, which Anuradha borrowed, is a back-test on a cohort whose outcome is already known. Gulmohar's 2024–25 cohort of 2,26,000 students yields the table below.

Behaviour band (2024–25 cohort)StudentsRenewedRenewal rate
< 20 study minutes/week58,00013,90024%
20–60 minutes/week, < 0.5 mock tests/week96,00033,60035%
20–60 minutes/week, ≥ 0.5 mock tests/week41,00023,80058%
> 60 minutes/week, < 0.5 mock tests/week18,0007,00039%
> 60 minutes/week, ≥ 0.5 mock tests/week13,0008,40065%

Exhibit A — renewal by behaviour band, Gulmohar Learning, 2024–25 paying cohort. Bands are defined on weeks 4–16 of the subscription to avoid contaminating the predictor with end-of-year exam-season behaviour.

Read the table by row pairs rather than by column. Holding minutes roughly constant, adding mock tests moves renewal from 35% to 58% and from 39% to 65% — a 23 to 26 point swing. Holding mock tests constant, tripling minutes moves renewal from 35% to 39% and from 58% to 65% — four to seven points. Minutes is not worthless; it is the weaker signal by a factor of roughly four, which is why Anuradha's instinct beat her CFO's. This is the crude analogue of the Prentice test: if the effect of more study runs mostly through mock tests, then conditional on mock-test frequency, minutes should carry little extra information about renewal — and in Gulmohar's data it carries a little, but not much. Nothing here rules out the reverse arrow: students who have already decided to stay may simply take more tests.

Step four: choose the denominator, knowing it is half the metric's definition. Per licensed seat (Hiranya's 11,800) is exogenous, fixed by contract; it cannot be gamed and it captures activation failure, but it moves in step changes at renewal. Per active seat (7,100) is endogenous — the product's own success at activating technicians changes it — which makes the ratio interpretable but treacherous, since anything that drives away marginal users flatters it. Per enrolled unit over a fixed window is the compromise: all seats licensed at the quarter's start, whatever they did afterwards. Experimentation teams arrive by another route: randomisation-unit denominators are safe, post-treatment denominators are not.

Step five: work out the arithmetic of the ratio itself, which is not innocent. A ratio of sums and a mean of ratios are different numbers. Gulmohar's base splits into 2,80,000 students averaging 42 minutes a week and a 30,000-strong repeat cohort averaging 105. The ratio of sums — total minutes over total subscribers — is (2,80,000 × 42 + 30,000 × 105) ÷ 3,10,000 = 1,49,10,000 ÷ 3,10,000 = 48.1 minutes. The unweighted mean of the two cohort ratios is (42 + 105) ÷ 2 = 73.5. Both are defensible; only one describes the typical student, and a dashboard that silently averages per-segment ratios reports a business that does not exist.

Step six: treat the ratio's variance properly when it enters an experiment. Because both numerator and denominator are random, the standard error of a ratio metric is not the standard error of the numerator. The delta method gives Var(X̄/Ȳ) ≈ (1/Ȳ²)[Var(X̄) − 2(X̄/Ȳ)Cov(X̄,Ȳ) + (X̄/Ȳ)²Var(Ȳ)]. The covariance term is what matters. When Gulmohar ran a fourteen-day test of a redesigned mock-test flow on 41,000 students, the naive computation reported a lift of 0.04 tests per subscriber per week, standard error 0.018 — p ≈ 0.03, ship it. The delta-method standard error, accounting for treatment also changing who counted as active, was 0.031 — p ≈ 0.21. The metric's definition and its statistical treatment are the same decision, made twice.

Figure 2 — the point estimate is identical; only the denominator's randomness is accounted for differently. One interval excludes zero, the other does not.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four claims, each testable, each applied to both protagonists. Claim one: a proxy is licensed only when the outcome's lag exceeds the decision cadence. Gulmohar passes decisively. Hiranya passes only weakly: Suhel can ask a customer's operations head how throughput feels, which is unsystematic but not eleven months slow, so Hiranya's proxies carry a weaker excuse for being wrong. Claim two: normalise when the denominator can move for reasons unrelated to the decision. Gulmohar's subscriber base grew 20% on marketing spend that had nothing to do with the product; without normalisation every product metric would have risen regardless of merit. Hiranya's seat count is fixed by contract within a quarter, so normalisation adds little within an account — but everything across accounts, since a 40-seat diagnostics chain and a 2,000-seat appliance network cannot be compared on totals. Claim three: a ratio is unsafe when its denominator is endogenous to the change being evaluated. Both fail this test on their current definitions, which is why both moved to enrolment-based denominators. Claim four: the idea is actively misleading when the denominator is itself the objective. If Gulmohar's goal for a quarter is acquisition into Tier-3 towns, minutes per subscriber falls by construction as less-intense new students dilute the base; judging acquisition by a per-user engagement ratio punishes it for succeeding. In that quarter the honest headline is a magnitude with a cohort split, and the ratio belongs in the appendix.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies hit the denominator-union problem. If Gulmohar launches a doubts-solving service alongside test prep, "minutes per subscriber" averages two populations of structurally different intensity, and the blend moves whenever the mix moves, independent of either product's health. Mature firms resolve this not with a cleverer blended metric but by refusing one: per-product ratios, a single company magnitude, and an explicit mix exhibit.

Two-sided businesses face the harder version. At Gathri Bazaar, a Jaipur-based handicrafts marketplace, orders per active buyer rose 14% in a quarter while orders per active seller fell 22%, because the platform had onboarded sellers faster than demand. Neither ratio is the business; the business is liquidity, captured by a match rate — the share of listings receiving an order within 30 days — a ratio whose two terms sit on opposite sides of the market. Marketplace teams learn to distrust any ratio whose terms come from the same side.

Regulated contexts invert the usual preference. Himmat Insurance Services, selling term cover under IRDAI conduct rules, cannot treat "policies sold per agent" as a north star: the regulator's interest is mis-selling, which shows up as thirteen-month persistency — a direct outcome it requires to be reported. Here the direct metric is mandated and available, and the proxy needs the justification. Regulated firms often run this discipline better than unregulated ones, for no reason more noble than that someone external checks their arithmetic.

Hardware-plus-software companies reconcile two clocks. Ganak Devices, selling a ₹6,500 water-quality monitor with a companion app, books revenue at sale, so its financial outcome is a magnitude with no natural denominator, while its retention outcome — whether the device still reports readings at month 18 — is a ratio over a cohort that takes eighteen months to close. The seam is where such firms quietly lose the argument: sales reports units, product reports connected-device ratios, and no forum compares them.

AI-native products break the counting assumption itself. Humraah Health, a triage assistant used by clinics in Nashik and Nagpur, found that its obvious ratio — resolved queries per active clinician — rewarded the model for answering confidently and penalised it for escalating, which is the opposite of what a triage tool should do. The fix was not a better denominator but a changed numerator: resolutions surviving a 72-hour no-escalation window. In AI products proxies decay fastest, because the system optimises against whatever it is scored on at a speed no organisation can match.

At the organisational seam, the common failure is that finance, product and sales each hold a defensible metric and nobody owns the translation between them. What mature companies actually do, whatever their metric charters say, is appoint one person — usually an analytics lead — accountable for the definition, with the right to refuse a slide.

6. Nuances that separate the expert

A blended ratio can fall while every segment rises. This is Simpson's paradox, and it is the single most expensive arithmetic fact in product analytics. Hiranya's quarter is exactly this case: metro technicians improved from 3.0 to 3.2 closes per day, non-metro from 4.5 to 4.7, and the blend fell from 4.00 to 3.63 because the mix shifted toward lower-throughput metro accounts. The tell is a ratio that moves sharply in a period when population composition also moved sharply; the obvious reading — performance declined — is wrong. Performance improved everywhere while the business sold into a harder segment.

Figure 3 — closes per active technician per day. The blended bar is a weighted average whose weights changed more than its components did.

The denominator is where gaming lives, not the numerator. Teams police numerators and let denominators drift, but the cheapest way to improve any per-user ratio is to shed marginal users. The tell is a ratio improving in a period when the denominator shrinks; the diagnostic is to recompute it on the prior period's frozen denominator. Gulmohar's minutes-per-subscriber would have read 51 rather than 48 had the 62,000 Tier-3 students acquired in November simply not been counted.

Proxies decay at a rate you can estimate. Decay is not a vague warning; it is a measurable slope. Gulmohar re-runs the back-test each quarter and tracks the renewal gap between the top and bottom mock-test bands. When that gap narrowed from 31 points to 19 after a pricing change brought in a different kind of student, the proxy had not become useless — it had become half as informative, and confidence in every roadmap decision should have loosened accordingly. Most teams treat validity as binary; experts treat it as a quantity with a trend.

Goodhart's law is about incentives, not about measurement. A proxy used to read the world stays honest far longer than the same proxy used to set a bonus. The tell is organisational, not statistical: ask whether anyone's compensation, promotion case or quarterly rating depends on the number. Hiranya's customer-success team had a variable component tied to weekly active seats, and unsurprisingly had built a habit of prompting technicians to log in on Fridays. The obvious remedy — remove the metric — is wrong; separate the scorecard metric from the steering metric and accept that the two will sometimes disagree in public.

The magnitude is not the naive metric; it is the one that pays salaries. Ratio-first orthodoxy has produced a generation of PMs who apologise for reporting totals. But Gulmohar plans question-bank production from total mock tests attempted, and Hiranya's infrastructure costs scale with total work orders. The distinction is not ratio-good, magnitude-bad: ratios adjudicate quality, magnitudes size commitments, and confusing the two questions is the error.

Changing a metric's definition is a change to the business, and must be dated. When Hiranya moved from active seats to enrolled seats, the ratio fell from 3.63 to 2.19 overnight with no change in the world. Experts publish a definition change the way a listed company publishes a restatement: both series shown for two periods, the change dated, the reason given. The tell of a weak practice is a dashboard whose historical numbers silently change when someone edits a query.

Composite indices buy sensitivity and sell interpretability. The surrogate-index literature is right that a weighted blend of five proxies predicts the outcome better than any one. It is also true that when a blended index moves 4%, nobody in the room can say what happened. Experts use composites for automated decisions — experiment readouts, model objectives — and single interpretable ratios for human forums, treating them as different instruments rather than pretending one serves both.

Correlation with the outcome does not license the proxy as a lever. Gulmohar's table shows mock-test takers renew more. It does not show that pushing a reluctant student into a mock test raises their renewal probability. The only clean test is an experiment that moves the proxy and observes the outcome — which reintroduces the eleven-month lag the proxy was invented to escape. This circularity is genuine and unresolved, and the honest expert says so rather than pretending the back-test settled it.

The right normalisation is often neither per-user nor per-total, but per-opportunity. Hiranya's most informative number turned out to be closes per assigned work order, because a technician's throughput is bounded by dispatch, not by software. Per-opportunity denominators — per session, per eligible transaction, per served impression — isolate the part of the outcome the product can actually influence, and their absence is the most common sign that a team has chosen a denominator by convention rather than by causal reasoning.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer subscription, the denominator is a person and the population is large and comparable, so per-user ratios are the default and the main risk is mix. In B2B and enterprise, the denominator is contested — seat, account or opportunity — and the outcome is a negotiated renewal one unhappy procurement head can override; enterprise PMs therefore hold usage ratios more loosely than consumer PMs find comfortable. Platforms and marketplaces need cross-side ratios, as Gathri Bazaar found, and are the one product type where a single north-star ratio is usually indefensible. In hardware and physical goods, the financial outcome is a magnitude realised at sale while the product outcome is a long-horizon ratio, and the two live in different organisations; the difference here is real and structural, not a matter of discipline. In AI products, the proxy's decay rate is the dominant consideration, because the system itself optimises against the measure. Across stages the difference is statistical power, not philosophy: a seed-stage company with 600 users cannot validate a proxy at all and should say so rather than dress a guess as a metric; only at scale does quarterly re-validation become affordable and necessary. What does not differ, despite frequent claims, is the logic — both face the same four questions with different amounts of evidence.

8. Three worked examples

Ganak Devices, and a ratio that was right. Ganak sold 74,000 monitors in FY25 at ₹6,500, and sales reported that number. Product reported devices still transmitting at day 540: 31% of the FY24 cohort. The installed transmitting base was therefore smaller than the cumulative unit count implied by a factor of three, and the ₹11 crore of subscription attach revenue the board had modelled was arithmetically impossible. The ratio did not contradict the magnitude; it reinterpreted it, and the forecast was cut to ₹4.1 crore before the miss rather than after.

Ikshu Beverages, and a proxy that failed. Ikshu, a cold-pressed juice brand selling through its own app and through modern trade, adopted repeat-purchase rate — repeat customers over customers acquired 90 days earlier — as its headline. It rose from 28% to 39% over three quarters and the team scaled spend accordingly. The failure had two parts. The denominator was acquisition 90 days prior, and acquisition had been cut sharply in the middle quarter, leaving a small, unusually high-intent cohort. And a subscription option launched in month two auto-counted as a repeat purchase, silently changing the numerator. Revenue per acquired customer, a magnitude the team had stopped reporting, had fallen 9%. The recovery was procedural: freeze the definition, restate eight quarters, split subscription from one-off repeats, and make revenue per acquired cohort a mandatory companion magnitude. The episode cost roughly ₹3 crore of misdirected spend and a quarter of board credibility — cheap only because someone asked the right question in month nine rather than month twenty.

Humraah Health, and a numerator repaired. After redefining resolution to require 72 hours without escalation, Humraah's headline ratio fell from 0.78 to 0.54 resolutions per clinician-session. Nothing had worsened; the earlier number had counted confident answers that clinics quietly overrode. The useful finding was that the gap between the two definitions — 24 points — was itself the best available measure of model overconfidence, and tracking it became more valuable than either ratio alone.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Five recur. Denominator shrinkage flattering a ratio announces itself as a per-user metric improving while totals stagnate; the diagnostic question is "what does this look like on last quarter's denominator," and caught late it produces a retention strategy built on the preferences of the users who stayed. Mix shift misread as performance change announces itself as a blended ratio moving more than any segment; the question is "which segments moved and by how much did their weights move," and caught late it triggers a remediation programme aimed at a problem that does not exist. Silent definition drift announces itself as a historical series that changes between two screenshots; the question is "when did this definition last change and who approved it," and caught late it destroys trust in every series. Proxy decay announces itself as a widening gap between the proxy's movement and the outcome's, visible only if both are tracked; the question is "when did we last re-estimate the proxy's predictive validity," and caught late it means a year of roadmap decisions made against a signal that had stopped meaning anything. Proxy converted into a target announces itself the day the number enters a compensation plan; the question is "whose bonus depends on this," and caught late it produces the most expensive outcome of all — a team that has successfully moved a number while the business it stood for went backwards.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether headline metrics should be composites. The surrogate-index position rests on real evidence that weighted blends predict long-run outcomes better than single signals, and on the practical observation that single ratios are too noisy to adjudicate individual features. It would be wrong if organisational interpretability turns out to matter more than statistical accuracy — that is, if a number nobody can explain fails to change behaviour no matter how predictive it is. The opposing position rests on exactly that claim, and neither side has evidence that settles it, because the outcome in question is organisational, not statistical.

Whether endogenous denominators are ever acceptable. The purist position — denominators must be fixed at randomisation or enrolment — is unanswerable on statistical grounds. The practitioner position is that per-active-user ratios are what product teams can actually feel and act on, and that a technically cleaner metric nobody uses is worse than a flawed one everybody understands. It would be wrong if a team could be shown to reach systematically worse decisions on enrolment denominators, and no one has shown that.

Whether proxies may be targets at all. Goodhart's law says no. But every operating cadence in every company runs on targets, and a steering metric with no target attached tends to get ignored. The permissive position, at its strongest, is that proxies may be targeted provided the target is paired with guardrails and re-validated; the prohibitionist position is that guardrails are always incomplete and the gaming finds the gap. Hiranya's Friday-login habit is one data point for the prohibitionists; the many firms running targeted proxies for years without disaster are data points for the other side.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can name the four quadrants. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They ask for the denominator before the number, every time, as a reflex rather than a gotcha. They hold a live estimate — not a belief but a number, with a date — of how well each proxy currently predicts the outcome, and they volunteer when that estimate has weakened, including when it weakens in a quarter they would otherwise have been congratulated for. And they are comfortable presenting a magnitude and a ratio that point in opposite directions, saying which question each answers and declining to collapse them into one verdict — the rarest behaviour, because it means tolerating in public the ambiguity most dashboards exist to hide.

12. What Anuradha and Suhel decided

Anuradha proposed, and Gulmohar's board accepted in February 2026, that mock tests completed per enrolled subscriber become the steering metric for the roadmap, reported alongside total study minutes as a capacity magnitude and alongside the quarterly re-estimated renewal gap between behaviour bands. Her argument to the CFO was not that his number was wrong but that it answered a different question: total minutes sizes the content pipeline, and the ratio decides which features live. She also committed to a holdout of 12,000 students who would receive no mock-test nudges, accepting the eleven-month wait, precisely because the back-test could not distinguish the causal arrow from the selection effect.

Suhel took the harder path. He presented both numbers to the customer, with the segment decomposition, and led with the finding that throughput had risen in every segment while the account's own hiring had shifted the mix. The ₹6.2 crore contract renewed. He then moved internal reporting to closes per assigned work order, froze the definition, restated four quarters, and removed weekly active seats from the customer-success incentive plan — over the objection of the revenue leader, who pointed out, correctly and with evidence, that it had been the team's most reliable early warning of churn.

Three questions for discussion. First: Anuradha's holdout will answer the causal question in eleven months, by which time the product will have changed; is a slow clean answer to yesterday's question worth more than a fast dirty answer to today's, and how would you decide? Second: Suhel removed a metric from an incentive plan that was demonstrably predictive of churn — was he right, and what would have to be true about the gaming's magnitude for the opposite call to be correct? Third: both companies chose a single steering ratio; under what circumstances is the honest answer that no single number should steer, and how would you defend that position to a board that wants one?

13. Going deeper

The GAME framework is the parent structure: goal, action, metric, evaluation. This topic is its metric step, and returning to GAME after reading this makes clear why the counting choice cannot be made before the action has been named. What makes a good metric supplies the criteria — comparable, understandable, ratio or rate, behaviour-changing — that the four-quadrant analysis here presupposes. Vanity vs actionable metrics is the older, blunter version of this distinction, and shows how much that version leaves out. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions determines which denominator is even available. North Star metric is where the composite-versus-interpretable disagreement of section ten plays out in organisational practice. Attention, transaction and productivity games explains why the same ratio means different things in three business models — Gulmohar plays an attention-adjacent game, Hiranya a productivity game. Breadth × depth × frequency supplies the decomposition that turns one engagement ratio into three levers, the natural next step once a ratio has been chosen.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Pragati Wealth: Counting SIPs

A teaching case. Pragati Wealth is a fictional company; the market, regulators and competitors around it are real.

1. The best quarter, and the memo about it

At a quarter past nine on the evening of Thursday, 8 January 2026, Meera Raghunathan was the last person on the fourth floor of Pragati Wealth's office in HSR Layout, Bengaluru. On her screen was a slide titled "Q3 FY26: our best quarter yet," and beside it a memo she had written and not yet sent.

The slide was accurate. Between October and December 2025, Pragati Wealth had registered 4.62 lakh new systematic investment plans, up 41 percent from the September quarter, the highest in the company's six-year history. The memo said that the number should not be the product team's target for FY27, and proposed something else in its place.

Meera was Head of Product. The annual planning offsite was on Monday, 12 January, at a hotel near Devanahalli, and the co-founder and chief executive, Aniruddh Sheth, had asked each function head to bring one primary metric for the year — "one number, owned by you, that we will read every week." Meera had until Monday morning to decide which number she would own.

2. Company background

Pragati Wealth was founded in 2019 to sell mutual funds to first-time investors outside the metros. Its proposition was narrow and had worked: a Hindi-, Marathi- and Kannada-capable app, a ₹500 minimum monthly SIP, onboarding that completed a SEBI-compliant KYC in under nine minutes, and a UPI AutoPay e-mandate set up through NPCI's rails so that the monthly debit needed no further action from the investor.

By December 2025 the company had 62 lakh registered users, 18.4 lakh investors with at least one live SIP, and ₹9,840 crore of assets under management. It earned a trail commission from asset managers, averaging 62 basis points a year on equity assets. It competed with Groww and Zerodha's Coin for the same first-time investor, with Paytm Money and ET Money on distribution reach, and with bank branches everywhere. AMFI's monthly industry data, which every investor and journalist read, reported gross SIP accounts added — the same magnitude that sat on Meera's slide.

The team had grown outward from Bengaluru. Fourteen engineers sat in Bengaluru and six in Pune; the mandate-and-payments squad was in Pune because two of its engineers had come from a Pune payment gateway. Lorenz Hartmann, the design lead, worked from Berlin and had redesigned the mandate flow twice. Preeti Balakrishnan, the company's only data scientist, worked from Toronto, which meant her analyses landed in Bengaluru inboxes at about seven in the morning. Shalini Nair ran customer success from Singapore and looked after the non-resident segment, including a Dubai-based construction group whose 2,300 Indian employees invested through a payroll tie-up — Pragati's single largest institutional relationship, worth ₹41 crore of AUM.

3. The situation

The 41 percent rise in registrations had a visible cause. Between 10 October and 20 November, around Navratri and Diwali, the growth team had spent ₹18.0 crore on a campaign built around a ₹500 "Diwali SIP", against ₹9.4 crore in the previous quarter. Kabir Ahluwalia, the VP Growth, had run it from Gurugram and considered it his best work.

Preeti's analysis, which had arrived on 2 January, told a different story about the same quarter. A registered SIP at Pragati becomes a real investment only when the first debit succeeds, typically between twenty and thirty-five days later, and the mandate has to clear the investor's bank. In the September quarter, 68.0 percent of registrations reached a successful first debit. In the December quarter, 61.0 percent did. Of those that did clear, the share still live after three consecutive monthly debits fell from 74.0 percent to a projected 59.0 percent — projected, because December's registrations would not complete three debits until March.

Put together, the two quarters had produced almost the same number of surviving SIPs: about 1.65 lakh in the September quarter and about 1.66 lakh in the December quarter. The ₹8.6 crore of extra marketing had bought registrations, not investors. Meera had checked the arithmetic twice, then asked Preeti to check it again.

4. The people

Aniruddh Sheth, co-founder and chief executive, split his week between Bengaluru and Mumbai. Pragati was six months from raising a Series D, and Aniruddh wanted a number that investors could compare with AMFI's published industry series. "Gross SIP accounts is the language of this market," he had told Meera in December. "If we invent our own metric, we spend the first twenty minutes of every meeting explaining it."

Kabir Ahluwalia, VP Growth in Gurugram, was measured on registrations and paid partly on them. He did not dispute Preeti's arithmetic. He disputed the inference: the December cohort was younger, poorer and newer to investing, so of course it converted worse, and it would be perverse to punish the team that had brought Pragati its first real presence in Indore, Nagpur and Kanpur.

Preeti Balakrishnan, data scientist in Toronto, had built the survival model and was the most cautious voice on it. Her point was practical: a three-month survival number cannot be a weekly metric, because it does not exist for three months. She had offered an intermediate — first-debit success within thirty-five days — which was observable quickly and correlated well with survival on the 2024 and 2025 cohorts.

Shalini Nair, customer success lead in Singapore, wanted whichever metric made mandate reliability somebody's problem. Her Dubai payroll relationship had generated forty-one complaints in December about debits failing on salary-credit day, and she had no one to escalate to, because no one's target moved when a mandate failed.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the case in miniature. Read from the top, the quarter is a triumph; read from the bottom, Pragati paid ₹1,084 for each investor it kept, nearly double the ₹570 of the previous quarter, to end with the same number of investors. Meera noticed that the two rows an outsider would quote — registrations and spend — were both magnitudes, and that every row that carried the diagnosis was a ratio.
